newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's top drug lord dead, U.S. says.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's top drug lord dead, U.S. says.

text.p: Mexico's most wanted drug lord, who eluded countless police raids, has died, reportedly from undergoing plastic surgery to alter his appearance, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) said on Sunday.

Mexican authorities spoke on Saturday night of the "probable death of the drug trafficker Amado Carrillo Fuentes" but said they needed more tests to confirm the identity of a man who died after plastic surgery and liposuction on Friday in a Mexico City clinic.

It was left to DEA chief Thomas Constantine to announce in Washington the death of Carrillo Fuentes, nicknamed "The Lord of the Skies" for his ability to fly jetloads of cocaine across Mexico for smuggling into the United States.

"The so-called 'Lord of the Skies' may have escaped earthly justice but I'm sure there is a special place in hell reserved for those like him who have destroyed countless human lives," the DEA chief said in a statement.
Neither he nor Mexican officials referred to the irony of one of the world's most wanted men dying of accidental causes in the Mexican capital while admitted to a public hospital.

Mexico is traditionally extremely secretive about drug issues. Authorities appeared anxious not to allow the bizarre death of their most wanted fugitive right under their noses to overshadow national elections held on Sunday.
"We have no information," insisted a spokesman for the Attorney General's office on Sunday afternoon when questioned about the DEA statement.
The family of the drug lord had been mourning his death since Friday night and lashed out at authorities on Saturday for refusing to hand over the body.

Hordes of smartly dressed men, some in snakeskin boots and cowboy hats, arrived in brand-new four-wheel-drive vehicles with darkened windows at the luxury Carrillo family ranch in the village of Guamuchilito in northwestern Mexico to deliver 8-foot (2.2-metre)-high floral wreaths and offer condolences.

The capo's mother, Aurora Fuentes de Carrillo, arrived sobbing with her three daughters at a funeral parlour in the state capital, Culiacan, on Saturday night to identify a body in a gray metal coffin.
"Yes, it's my son," she cried to waiting reporters.

Moments later, scores of heavily armed police, some in plainclothes, others toting submachine guns, descended on the funeral parlour. After a furious argument with the family, they removed the body under heavy security and shipped it aboard an aircraft at Sinaloa's main airport, Culiacan.

Apparently determined to hold on to the body of the man it never caught while he was alive, the Attorney General's Office refused on Sunday to say even where Carrillo's corpse was. The DEA said, however, it had gone to Mexico City for DNA testing.

In the only offical Mexican information so far, the Attorney General's Office said in a statement on Saturday night that a man had been admitted to the Santa Monica hospital, a small, exclusive clinic in Mexico City's smart Polanco district, on Thursday under the name of Antonio Flores Montes for extensive facial plastic surgery and liposuction.
After an eight-hour operation on Friday, the patient was taken to Room 407 of the hospital, where a duty doctor found him dead in bed at 6 p.m., the statement said.
A certificate in the name of Antonio Flores, aged 42, gave the cause of death as a heart attack. The body was flown on Saturday morning to Culiacan and sent to the funeral parlour.

The Attorney General's Office said it had carried out an autopsy and fingerprint tests. "Although from the tests carried out so far there are indications that the body which allegedly belongs to Antonio Flores Montes is really that of Amado Carrillo Fuentes, the (office) cannot, at the moment, affirm this with total certainty," it said.

Carrillo, believed to be 42 years old, was born into a poor peasant family but rose fast to become a drug superstar. As Mexican cartels evolved from being middlemen for Colombian cocaine shipments to big traffickers in their own right, his cartel, centred on the Mexican border town of Ciudad Juarez, gained in might.

"Amado Carrillo-Fuentes was arguably the most powerful drug trafficker in Mexico," DEA chief Constantine said in his statement confirming Carrillo's death. "The disruption his death will cause among Mexican drug trafficking organisations will be significant."

Mexico's former anti-drug chief, Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, was jailed in February on charges he had taken bribes from Carrillo, including a luxury apartment for his mistress, armoured cars, scrambler phones and money.

The last confirmed sighting of the capo was in January, when a videotape showed him attending the wedding of his sister at the Guamuchilito ranch. Police and troops raided the reception after the ceremony but Carrillo escaped, apparently after being tipped off about the raid.
